Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 80 min read (16055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~80 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that heterochromatin typically represses genes1,2, yet some genes paradoxically require it for activation3,4,5,6,7.
  • In a recent development, histone H3 lysine 9 (H3 K9) trimethylation, a canonical post-translational modification of constitutive heterochromatin, is known to spread over large genomic territories and repress gene expression9.
  • The vertebrate clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus provides a striking example of a large gene family whose expression has been proposed to require escape from a heterochromatic environment10,11,12,13.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that heterochromatin typically represses genes1,2, yet some genes paradoxically require it for activation3,4,5,6,7. How can the same chromatin environment both silence and promote transcription? Here we address this question by interrogating the clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus, where subsets of genes are stochastically expressed while most remain silent8. In neurons, stochastic and combinatorial expression of Pcdh genes generates unique cell-surface barcodes required for self–non-self discrimination and neural circuit assembly8. By combining RNA labelling of Pcdh genes and neurodevelopmental cell types with single-molecule chromatin tracing and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, we find that a compact heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh genes forms as these genes become activated during development. Pcdh transcription occurs within the compact domain and reads through downstream genes, and distal enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters. Genetic perturbations in mice suggest that opposing genome folding forces cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote stochastic Pcdh expression. Specifically, while DNA loop extrusion allows enhancers to breach heterochromatin and find target promoters, heterochromatin-driven compartmentalization supports an expanded enhancer–promoter search space. These findings shed light on a process foundational to the development of vertebrate nervous systems and suggest a mechanism for how transcription can occur within seemingly silent chromatin environments.

In a recent development, histone H3 lysine 9 (H3 K9) trimethylation, a canonical post-translational modification of constitutive heterochromatin, is known to spread over large genomic territories and repress gene expression9. These defining properties of heterochromatin were recognized in classic position–effect variegation studies in Drosophila during the 1930s, in which euchromatic genes placed near domains with trimethylated H3 K9 (H3K9me3) became transcriptionally silenced1,2. However, subsequent discovery of genes whose expression depends on their residence within heterochromatin revealed that this conflict is not absolute. For example, expression of the light (lt) and rolled (rl) genes in flies requires their position within pericentromeric heterochromatin3,4,5. In mice and humans, proper expression of olfactory receptor (OR) and KRAB domain-containing zinc-finger protein (KZFP) genes also depends on H3K9me3 heterochromatin6,7. These ‘escapee’ genes suggest the existence of specialized regulatory strategies that allow transcription to occur within, or despite, heterochromatin, raising fundamental questions about when heterochromatin facilitates versus restrains gene expression.

The vertebrate clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus provides a striking example of a large gene family whose expression has been proposed to require escape from a heterochromatic environment10,11,12,13. Pcdh genes are expressed predominantly in neurons, where they govern neuronal self–non-self discrimination and circuit formation8. In individual neurons, only a small subset of Pcdh genes are expressed, whereas most remain silent8. Because selection of Pcdh genes is random and combinatorial14,15,16,17, this process generates extraordinary cell surface protein isoform diversity that marks each neuron with a unique identity, or ‘barcode’. Neurites presenting the same Pcdh barcode recognize and avoid one another, thereby preventing self-adhesion, whereas neurites presenting distinct Pcdh barcodes do not self-recognize and can interact18,19,20. Consistent with their critical role in neural circuit assembly, genetic variants in Pcdh genes are associated with neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, including autism spectrum disorder21,22 and schizophrenia23.

In mice, there are 58 Pcdh genes distributed across three tandemly arranged clusters—α (Pcdha), β (Pcdhb) and γ (Pcdhg)—spanning roughly 1 megabase of DNA on chromosome 18 (ref. 24) (Fig. 1a). Pcdha genes are regulated by the HS5-1 enhancer located downstream of the Pcdha cluster, whereas Pcdhb and Pcdhg genes are regulated by the HS18-22 and HS16-17 enhancers, respectively, located downstream of the Pcdhg cluster25 (Fig. 1a). The Pcdha and Pcdhg genes are further subdivided into ‘alternate’ and ‘c-type’ isoforms24 (Fig. 1a). Pcdh genes and their promoters are marked by H3 K9 trimethylation and CpG DNA methylation (5mC)10,13,26. Stochastic Pcdh gene choice requires promoter DNA demethylation driven by cohesin-mediated enhancer–promoter interactions, with promoter demethylation leading to CTCF binding and sustained transcription of the respective Pcdh gene10,13,15,27,28. Although these findings have identified how Pcdh promoters escape DNA methylation, they do not address how euchromatic Pcdh enhancers navigate H3K9me3 heterochromatin to activate silent Pcdh promoters. Several questions remain unanswered. Specifically, do stochastic enhancer–promoter interactions occur within heterochromatin? Is Pcdh transcription carried out within a heterochromatic environment otherwise programmed to suppress gene activity, or must Pcdh loci escape this environment to transcribe? And, does heterochromatin contribute to the stochasticity of Pcdh promoter choice?

In a recent development, to answer these questions, we sought a single-molecule view of Pcdh locus architecture during development that included the positioning of active and inactive promoters. Until now, most insights into this relationship have come from bulk genomic analyses. At a locus where only a few genes are active while most remain silent, bulk measurements mainly reflect the non-chosen genes, effectively averaging out the features of the chosen ones. To circumvent this limitation, we used optical reconstruction of chromatin architecture (ORCA), a single-molecule chromatin tracing assay29, in olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) of the mouse olfactory epithelium (OE). We selected OSNs for three reasons. First, they undergo multiple stages of development and constantly regenerate, such that each stage is present within the OE simultaneously. Second, Pcdh gene expression is developmentally regulated during OSN maturation15,20, with approximately one gene per cluster expressed from each allele in mature OSNs (mOSNs) (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Third, stochastic expression of Pcdh genes has a critical role in OSN axon wiring and odour map formation20,30,31.

Sources indicate that we designed ORCA probes that tile the Pcdh locus in 90 10-kilobase bins, omitting repetitive and GC-poor regions (Fig. 1a). ORCA probes were validated in OE sections from mice in which mOSNs were genetically labelled (Extended Data Fig. 2a). We visualized ORCA data as contact frequency matrices, which depict the frequency that each pair of locus positions (bins along the Pcdh locus) falls within a specified three-dimensional (3D) distance across all imaged traces. We set this threshold near the average distance between adjacent locus positions in an experiment. The contact frequency map obtained from ORCA correlated strongly with chromosome conformation capture Hi-C data of the same genomic bins from sorted mOSNs (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c, Pearson’s r = 0.87), and the correlation remained high across a sweep of ORCA contact thresholds (Extended Data Fig. 2d). ORCA data from whole OE tissue also remained consistent across separate experiments (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f, Pearson’s r = 0.98) and indicated good detection efficiency across locus positions (Extended Data Fig. 2g). These results demonstrate that ORCA faithfully captures Pcdh locus architecture.

To study how Pcdh locus architecture changes during Pcdh gene activation and neuronal maturation, we combined ORCA imaging of Pcdh DNA with RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) labelling of the five major OSN developmental cell stages: horizontal basal cells (HBCs), globose basal cells (GBCs), immediate neuronal precursors (INPs), immature OSNs (iOSNs) and mOSNs (Fig. 1c). This lineage spawns from the mitotic HBC population located near the basal surface of the OE. As OSNs progress along their developmental axis, these cells migrate towards the apical surface of the OE (Fig. 1c). RNA labelling of marker genes for each stage reflected this basal-to-apical migration (Fig. 1d). We also stained samples with fluorescently tagged wheat germ agglutinin (WGA), a lectin that binds cell membranes, to obtain 3D segmentations of cells in the OE (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We mapped both RNA and Pcdh DNA puncta to these segmentations, then classified ORCA traces (that is, individual DNA paths) into different developmental stages on the basis of the RNA signal of the cells in which they resided (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c).

The contact frequency maps for each stage of OSN development illustrated two trends. First, stripes denoting contacts between Pcdh enhancers and their target promoters became more prominent as cells matured (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1d–f). Second, contacts between locus positions containing Pcdhb genes and the alternate genes from the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, as well as the 60-kilobase stretch upstream of the Pcdha genes, increased (Fig. 1e,f). Subtracting the contact frequency map of each developmental stage from the mOSN map emphasized that these inter-cluster contacts constituted the most pronounced changes in locus architecture over development (Fig. 1e).

Industry observers note that the formation of these inter-cluster contact domains was reminiscent of the checkerboard pattern created by compartmentalization of active and repressed chromatin domains seen on Hi-C maps32. Given that this compartmentalization is mainly driven by homotypic interactions between heterochromatic regions of the genome, we hypothesized that the locus regions engaging in these contacts would have histone marks characteristic of heterochromatin. To investigate this possibility, we performed quantitative native chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (nChIP–seq) for H3K9me3 in FACS-isolated HBCs and mOSNs. In HBCs, the Pcdh locus was lightly coated in H3K9me3, with H3K9me3 levels increasing roughly threefold in mOSNs (Fig. 1g,h). Furthermore, in mOSNs, two major stretches of enriched H3K9me3 emerged separated by regions devoid of H3K9me3 between and beyond them (Fig. 1g). Specifically, the DNA regions of the Pcdh locus that engaged in inter-cluster contacts over OSN development became heavily coated with H3K9me3, whereas regions of the locus containing Pcdh c-type genes and enhancers remained free of H3K9me3 (Fig. 1e,g). We hereafter refer to the H3K9me3-marked chromatin regions engaging in inter-cluster contacts as the ‘heterochromatin domain’ of the Pcdh locus. This definition indicates the spatial arrangement of the regions within the Pcdh locus that are marked by H3K9me3 in OSNs. We refer to the regions of the locus not marked by H3K9me3 containing Pcdh c-type genes and enhancers as euchromatin.

Recent findings suggest that to understand the positioning of the heterochromatin domain within the architecture of the Pcdh locus, we calculated the distance of each locus position to the geometric centre of its respective trace and examined the median over all traces across each stage of development. All locus positions moved closer to the geometric centre as cells matured, indicating a general compaction of the locus (Fig. 1i). Layered on top of this trend, locus positions belonging to the heterochromatin domain moved closest to the centre (Fig. 1i, boxed regions), whereas euchromatic regions remained further in the periphery. To better quantify the degree of compaction of the heterochromatin domain, we measured its radius of gyration (Rg), a metric commonly used to describe the volume of a polymer, and found that Rg decreases as neurons mature (Fig. 1j). Surprisingly, as compaction increases, so does the number of genes expressed per cell from within the domain (Fig. 1j). We further visualized these changes in locus architecture by plotting individual traces coloured by regions that become heterochromatic or euchromatic over development and by examining single-molecule distance maps (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4). Despite heterogeneity across traces, the formation of the domain was evident: in HBCs, both regions tended to occupy large and intermixed volumes, whereas in mOSNs, the regions segregated, with heterochromatin forming a dense, more centrally located domain and euchromatin occupying more open volumes in the periphery (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4).

According to recent reports, overall, these results indicate that in neural stem cells, the Pcdh locus is lightly coated with H3K9me3 heterochromatin, yet open and intermixed, with a compact heterochromatin domain forming in its centre as cells mature into post-mitotic neurons (Fig. 1l). Counterintuitively, the formation of this compact structure coincides with activation of Pcdh genes (Fig. 1j).

It has been revealed that these results could be explained by the presence of two distinct subpopulations—actively transcribing loci that transiently lose heterochromatin and silent loci that do not. Alternatively, actively transcribing loci could retain heterochromatin and their compacted architecture. Because our bulk measurements of H3K9me3 by nChIP–seq could not distinguish between these two possibilities, we turned to stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM) to measure H3K9me3 in single cells. We combined STORM for H3K9me3 with RNA FISH labelling of Pcdh isoforms and OSN cell types, as well as ORCA imaging of DNA, to test for colocalization of heterochromatin with transcribing Pcdh alleles (Fig. 2a). We used RNA probes against 11 Pcdh isoforms and confirmed their specificity for their target isoforms in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b).

In a recent development, overlaying Pcdh RNA staining on Pcdh DNA loci labelled by ORCA revealed DNA traces that colocalized with RNA puncta (Extended Data Fig. 6a). By measuring distances between Pcdh loci and Pcdh RNA puncta, we identified a data-driven distance threshold below which RNA transcripts could be classified as nascent (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c). RNA puncta within this threshold were brighter than those beyond it, consistent with nascent transcriptional bursting33 (Extended Data Fig. 6d).

We then examined the spatial relationship between transcribing Pcdh DNA loci and H3K9me3 STORM signal in mOSNs. Remarkably, we observed many examples of nascent transcription occurring at Pcdh loci that colocalized with H3K9me3 STORM (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Plotting the ORCA traces of these loci alongside H3K9me3 STORM localizations revealed transcribing promoters spatially residing within heterochromatin (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 7a).

In a recent development, to assess whether STORM captured a nuclear enrichment of H3K9me3 over the Pcdh locus, we quantified the number of H3K9me3 localizations surrounding Pcdh loci relative to randomized positions within the same nuclei. The median number of H3K9me3 localizations detected around Pcdh DNA loci exceeded that of randomized positions in 999 of 1,000 simulations (empirical P = 0.002) (Fig. 2c). We performed the same analyses on Tex15 loci, which are not marked by H3K9me3 as assayed by bulk nChIP–seq (Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). We used Tex15 nascent RNA transcripts as proxies for Tex15 DNA positions (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). In contrast to Pcdh loci, Tex15 loci did not show an enrichment for H3K9me3 (empirical P = 0.292) (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Furthermore, we observed more Tex15 loci lacking any H3K9me3 signal compared with Pcdh loci (Extended Data Fig. 7e).

It has been revealed that we next asked whether Pcdh transcription was associated with reduced local H3K9me3 signal and domain compaction by first dividing loci into those with or without detectable nascent transcription, the latter of which we hereafter refer to as non-transcribing. We then measured the number of H3K9me3 STORM localizations around these loci and the Rg of their heterochromatin domains by ORCA. Surprisingly, transcribing Pcdh loci had slightly higher H3K9me3 STORM signal and slightly more compact heterochromatin domains relative to non-transcribing loci (Fig. 2d,e). Furthermore, transcription of individual Pcdh genes was associated neither with a change in H3K9me3 STORM signal around transcribing promoters, at the resolution of our assay, nor with a change in heterochromatin domain compaction (Fig. 2f,g).

Overall, these analyses indicate that transcription of Pcdh loci can occur in H3K9me3-rich nuclear territories and does not disrupt the heterochromatin domain of the locus.

In a recent development, these data prompted us to further evaluate features of a transcribing Pcdh locus. To do that, we expanded the design of our RNA probes to a total of 31 Pcdh genes that highlighted appreciable staining and specificity (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). We noted that nascently transcribing RNA puncta often colocalized with other Pcdh RNAs of the same cluster (Fig. 3a), and more nascent puncta were detected for progressively downstream isoforms at the Pcdha and Pcdhg, but not Pcdhb, clusters (Fig. 3b). Meanwhile, mature transcript levels measured by bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) remained relatively flat across all clusters (Fig. 3b). We reasoned that these results could reflect nascent transcription of Pcdha and Pcdhg genes that reads through downstream isoforms (Fig. 3c). Yet, the number of nascent Pcdh RNAs detected at a locus was not associated with changes in heterochromatin domain Rg (Fig. 3d), indicating that this putative transcriptional readthrough occurs without domain decompaction.

According to recent reports, to identify features of locus architecture associated with transcription, we subtracted the contact frequency maps of non-transcribing loci from the maps of transcribing loci in mOSNs. This revealed an enrichment of enhancer–promoter contacts in transcribing loci (Fig. 3e–g), which was further supported by an increase in transcription probability as a function of enhancer–promoter proximity (Extended Data Fig. 8). For Pcdha and Pcdhg genes, these enhancer–promoter contact enrichments included promoters upstream of the transcribing isoform, and the magnitude of enrichment experienced by each promoter diminished when filtering on transcription of progressively downstream isoforms (Fig. 3e,g). By contrast, Pcdhb promoters had more local enhancer-contact enrichments upon transcription (Fig. 3f).

It has been revealed that together, these data indicate that at the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, transcription of chosen promoters reads through downstream genes. This pattern is consistent with splicing of Pcdha and Pcdhg variable exons to three small constant exons located 3′ of these clusters34, and was not observed at the Pcdhb cluster, which lacks constant exons. Furthermore, these data indicate that Pcdh gene choice is driven by highly specific enhancer–promoter interactions across this multi-gene, multi-enhancer locus.

We next asked where Pcdh transcription and enhancer–promoter interactions occur within the spatial architecture of the locus (Fig. 1l) and, in particular, whether transcribing promoters remain within or exit the heterochromatin domain. To assess the positioning of transcribing promoters, we measured the distances between promoters and heterochromatic locus positions in the presence and absence of transcription in mOSNs (Fig. 4a). These distances did not change during transcription (Fig. 4a). On the other hand, distances between promoters and euchromatic locus positions decreased during transcription (Fig. 4a). This effect seemed driven by decreased distances between promoters and enhancers upon transcription (Fig. 4b). These results indicate that enhancer–promoter contacts associated with transcription bring euchromatic locus positions closer to the heterochromatin domain, but neither these contacts nor transcription itself cause transcribing promoters to exit the domain. Plotting transcription probability as a function of a promoter’s distance to the heterochromatin centre supported this conclusion, as promoters were most likely to be transcribing at distances within the median Rg of the heterochromatin domain (Fig. 4c).

For promoter–EC distances: P = 8.98 × 10−5. b, Median distances between Pcdh promoters and their respective enhancers in non-transcribing and transcribing traces. Each dot represents one Pcdh promoter–enhancer pair, with paired points connected by grey lines. Black bars, median across promoter–enhancer pairs for each transcription state. P = 0.019. Significance in a and b was assessed across isoforms or promoter–enhancer pairs using a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. *P < 0.05, ****P < 0.0001. c, Transcription probability as a function of promoter distance to the centre of the heterochromatin domain. Grey bars, number of promoter-to-heterochromatin centre measurements per bin. Dashed line, median heterochromatin domain Rg across all traces. Bin size, 50 nm. Error bars, 95% Wilson binomial confidence intervals. For a–c, analyses included 28 Pcdh isoforms across 16,399 ORCA traces from mOSNs. d, Example ORCA traces of transcribing Pcdha3, Pcdhb16 and Pcdhga2 loci with and without enhancer–promoter contacts. The transcribed Pcdh gene is labelled in blue in each trace.

To further dissect the positioning of enhancers and promoters relative to the heterochromatin and euchromatin compartments of the locus during contact, we calculated the distances of each locus position to the centre of the heterochromatin domain (dHC) and the centre of the euchromatic region housing the cluster-specific enhancer(s) of that position (dEC) (Extended Data Fig. 9a). We examined Pcdhb16 as a case study. In non-transcribing traces and transcribing traces without enhancer–promoter contacts, Pcdhb16 was closer to the heterochromatin centre than the euchromatin centre, whereas its enhancer HS18-22 showed the opposite relationship (Extended Data Fig. 9a). In Pcdhb16-transcribing traces with enhancer–promoter contacts, Pcdhb16 and its enhancer HS18-22 were more equidistant to the two centres (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Further evaluation of the equidistant state showed that the dHC of both promoter and enhancer decreased during contact, but that the enhancer dHC decreased by a greater magnitude (Extended Data Fig. 9b), consistent with promoters remaining within the heterochromatin domain during contact and the enhancers approaching the domain to engage promoters (Fig. 4a,b). Extending these analyses to all other Pcdh genes stained for showed similar positionings of transcribing Pcdh promoters and cognate enhancers relative to their compartment centres: when in contact, promoters and enhancers became more equidistant to the two centres; when not in contact, promoters were closer to the heterochromatin centre than the euchromatin centre, whereas enhancers were closer to the euchromatin centre (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Quantifying the percentage of transcribing traces with and without enhancer–promoter contacts revealed the latter state to be more prevalent (Extended Data Fig. 9e), indicating that promoters transcribe at positions closer to the heterochromatin centre, and that Pcdh transcription can be sustained in the absence of enhancer engagement.

Individual traces reflected the above behaviours. Transcribing promoters remained within the heterochromatin domain, and enhancers approached the domain to engage promoters (Fig. 4d).

Recent findings suggest that lastly, we investigated the genome folding mechanisms that establish Pcdh locus architecture and how this architecture supports stochastic Pcdh gene choice. The wild-type (WT) locus architecture is defined by stripes corresponding to enhancer–promoter contacts and by inter-cluster contacts within the heterochromatin domain (Fig. 1e). To abolish enhancer–promoter contacts, we conditionally removed Rad21, the kleisin subunit of the cohesin protein complex, using an Omp-ires-cre;Rad21fl/fl;tdTomatofl/fl (Rad21 cKO) mouse (Extended Data Fig. 10a). To perturb heterochromatin compaction, we conditionally deleted Setdb1, the SET domain bifurcated histone methyltransferase 1, which catalyses di- and trimethylation of H3K9, using an Omp-ires-cre;Setdb1fl/fl;tdTomatofl/fl (Setdb1 cKO) mouse (Extended Data Fig. 10a). We confirmed knockout of Rad21 and Setdb1 in mOSNs by immunofluorescence (Extended Data Fig. 10b), then performed ORCA in both mouse models.

Rad21 deletion abolished enhancer–promoter contacts as evidenced by a loss of stripes (Fig. 5a), consistent with previous reports10,13,15,27. By contrast, Setdb1 deletion resulted in a loss of inter-cluster contacts (Fig. 5a), which was accompanied by an approximately 40% reduction of H3K9me3 over the heterochromatin domain (Fig. 5b,c and Extended Data Fig. 10c). Furthermore, separation between heterochromatic and euchromatic regions of the locus increased in Rad21 cKO but decreased in Setdb1 cKO (Fig. 5d), whereas the relative size of the heterochromatin domain increased in Setdb1 cKO but decreased in Rad21 cKO (Fig. 5e).

Each black dot represents one biological replicate (WT: n = 6; Setdb1 cKO: n = 3). Data were combined across three independent experiments for WT and two independent experiments for Setdb1 cKO. Bars indicate means. Significance was assessed using Welch’s unpaired t-test, P = 0.007. d, Separation scores for the HC and EC regions of the locus. In the schematic, red regions represent heterochromatin and grey regions represent euchromatin. e, HC domain size as a fraction of total locus volume in terms of Rg. For d and e, distributions are shown as violin plots. Horizontal lines and numbers indicate medians. Significance was assessed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Adjusted P values for Rad21 cKO versus WT, WT versus Setdb1 cKO and Rad21 cKO versus Setdb1 cKO, respectively: P = 1.5 × 10−103, P = 3.6 × 10−101 and P < 1 × 10−230 in d and P = 1.1 × 10−23, P = 2.3 × 10−71 and P = 2.6 × 10−229 in e. **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001. f, ORCA traces from each condition with the heterochromatin domain and Pcdh enhancers labelled. g, Percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh gene across genotypes. Pcdhb1 is excluded.h, Change in percentage of mOSNs expressing Pcdha genes as a function of each gene’s distance to the HS5-1 enhancer in Rad21 cKO relative to WT. i, Change in percentage of mOSNs expressing Pcdha genes as a function of each gene’s distance to the heterochromatin domain boundary determined by nChIP–seq at the Pcdha cluster in Setdb1 cKO relative to WT.

Individual traces reflected these structural changes. Single molecules demonstrated distancing of Pcdh enhancers from the heterochromatin domain in Rad21 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by changes in the distance of each locus position relative to the heterochromatin domain centre (Extended Data Fig. 10d). Meanwhile, the heterochromatin domain seemed less compact and more intermixed with euchromatin in Setdb1 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by an increase in the entropy of each locus position in Setdb1 cKO (Extended Data Fig. 10e). These data suggest that Pcdh enhancers require cohesin to approach the heterochromatin domain and contact target promoters, whereas heterochromatin keeps the promoters in a compact and ordered environment.

To evaluate how these changes in Pcdh locus architecture affect stochastic Pcdh gene expression, we performed single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq). Ablation of Rad21 resulted in widespread downregulation of Pcdh expression in favour of Pcdhac2, the Pcdha gene most proximal to the HS5-1 enhancer, which also resides in euchromatin (Fig. 5g,h and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). This gain in expression of enhancer-proximal Pcdh genes was not observed at the Pcdhg cluster, suggesting distinct enhancer–promoter specificities at the two clusters (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). By contrast, ablation of Setdb1 resulted in upregulation of Pcdha10–12 and Pcdhgb6–b7, the genes closest to the heterochromatin–euchromatin boundaries at the locus (Fig. 5g,i and Extended Data Fig. 10f,h). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies reflected these expression changes in both genotypes (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j).

Sources indicate that these results indicate that DNA loop extrusion and heterochromatin compaction cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote an unbiased enhancer–promoter search space at the locus. While cohesin is required for Pcdh enhancers to gain access to the heterochromatin domain housing Pcdh promoters, the compaction of the domain expands the ability of the enhancers to find target promoters. Thus, although generally viewed as antagonistic processes35, both cohesin and heterochromatin-driven chromatin compartmentalization are indispensable for proper Pcdh expression.

Here we show that heterochromatin spatially partitions the Pcdh locus into a compacted domain housing Pcdh promoters and multiple open regions housing Pcdh enhancers. Transcription from chosen promoters occurs within the heterochromatin domain, and enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Counterintuitively, Pcdh transcription can read through hundreds of kilobases without dissolving the compacted state of the locus (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We further demonstrate that Pcdh locus architecture and proper Pcdh expression are achieved through cooperation between heterochromatin-mediated compaction and cohesin-mediated DNA loop extrusion.

Sources indicate that our findings challenge the prevailing view that heterochromatin is a physically inaccessible chromatin structure. Heterochromatin compaction was initially proposed to sterically hinder the transcriptional machinery and thereby repress gene expression36,37. However, rather than acting as an impenetrable barrier, our data indicate that heterochromatin can support active transcription while retaining a compact 3D organization. These findings add to a growing body of evidence suggesting that heterochromatin is not intrinsically inaccessible and can support transcription. For example, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-dense centromeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin are actively transcribed and accumulate abundant RNA despite their highly condensed appearance38. Furthermore, transcription can stabilize H3K9me3-modifying enzymes39,40,41, and dense heterochromatin nonetheless allows passage of transcription factors42 and large macromolecules43, including RNA polymerase II (ref. 44).

According to recent reports, these observations have motivated an alternative model of heterochromatin organization, wherein domain-scale compaction emerges from frequent intra-domain interactions that serve to reinforce the epigenetic state of the domain rather than directly silence the underlying DNA through steric exclusion. By this model, distal genomic loci are brought into proximity by the activity of heterochromatin reader and writer proteins, as readers bound to heterochromatin marks on one chromatin fibre might promote deposition of the same modification by writers on another fibre. This 3D reader–writer activity establishes a positive feedback loop that reinforces the heterochromatic state of the domain. Heterochromatin compaction thus functions to concentrate this feedback, ensuring it acts primarily back on the existing heterochromatin to stabilize its epigenetic state, rather than spreading or diluting to neighbouring euchromatin45,46.

According to recent reports, although heterochromatin has been proposed to be important for epigenetic memory at the Pcdh locus11,12, we found that chosen Pcdh promoters do not segregate from flanking promoters retaining the silent state, contrasting with the behaviour of chosen promoters in H3K27me3 heterochromatin29,47. This unexpected organization argues against domain-scale spatial segregation as a primary mechanism for heterochromatin-mediated memory of Pcdh gene choice. Instead, these data suggest that a more local compartmentalization of active and inactive genes might develop, with biophysically distinct microcompartments, or ‘pockets’, of active chromatin containing expressed genes forming within the heterochromatin domain. This model is consistent with the presence of both highly dynamic and more stable HP1 populations within the same heterochromatin environment48 and structural heterogeneity of heterochromatin compartments, as revealed by recent single-molecule footprinting49 and chromatin tracing46 studies.

Lastly, beyond classical examples of heterochromatic genes, such as the lt and rl genes in Drosophila3,4,5, the intermixed spatial organization of active and inactive genes within H3K9me3-enriched chromatin domains discussed here may reflect a more general property of gene regulation within heterochromatic territories—with particular relevance to genes arranged in clusters, such as OR6 and KZFP genes7. We propose that domain-scale spatial segregation of active and inactive genes might not be required at these clusters to accommodate and maintain expression of subsets of genes within a more broadly repressive chromatin domain. Furthermore, as we have shown here for Pcdh genes, these loci might also require the coordinated integration of genome folding mechanisms across scales—from higher-order heterochromatin compartmentalization to enhancer–promoter interactions mediated by various looping factors50—to achieve genomic architectures required for precise and selective gene activation.

In summary, our findings illustrate how seemingly silent chromatin domains can coordinate gene expression and invite a reconceptualization of heterochromatin from a singularly repressive chromatin environment to one that can, when properly configured, permit active transcription.

In a recent development, mice were perfused with 30 ml of ice-cold PBS followed by 30 ml of freshly prepared, ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Tissue from the mouse OE was dissected and incubated in 4% PFA with gentle rocking at 4 °C for 6 h. Tissue was then transferred to 30% sucrose in 1 × PBS, incubated with gentle rocking at 4 °C until sunk, then embedded in OCT. For ORCA experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 6 μm onto glass coverslips (Biooptechs, 40-1313-03191) coated with chromium potassium gelatin. Slides were coated as described previously52. For immunohistochemistry experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 20 μm onto Superfrost Plus slides (Fisherbrand, 1255015). ORCA coverslips were stored at −80 °C until use; immunohistochemistry slides were stored at −20 °C until use.

Industry observers note that for a breakdown of all ORCA-related experiments in the present study, see Supplementary Table 4. The genomic coordinates of the ORCA barcodes tiling the Pcdh locus are listed in Supplementary Table 5.

In a recent development, RNA and DNA probes were designed and hybridized as previously described52, with minor modifications as follows. Briefly, for combined RNA/DNA imaging experiments, RNA probes were hybridized and imaged first. Tissue sections mounted on coverslips were fixed in freshly prepared 4% PFA at room temperature for 10 min, followed by three washes in 1 × PBS. Sections were then permeabilized for 10 min at room temperature in 1% Triton X in 1 × PBS, followed by two washes with 1 × PBS. Next, sections were incubated for 5 min at room temperature in a protease solution consisting of 0.1 mg ml−1 pepsin (Sigma Aldrich, 501784863) in 10 mM HCl and washed twice in 0.1 M glycine in 1 × PBS to improve RNA hybridization efficiency. Sections were then cleared in 8% sodium dodecyl sulfate at room temperature for 10 min and washed three times in 2 × SSC, reducing background fluorescence. Following clearing, sections were incubated in Hybridization Buffer (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 0.1% Tween) for 35 min at room temperature. Then, 2,500 ng of primary RNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 10% dextran sulfate, 0.1% Tween) were added to the sections, covered with coverglass and incubated overnight (12–20 h) at 42 °C. The following morning, samples were washed twice for 10 min in 2 × SSC at 42 °C, washed once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then imaged. After RNA imaging, samples were re-fixed in 4% PFA for 5 min at room temperature, washed three times in 2 × SSC, re-permeabilized for 10 min in 1% Triton X-100 at room temperature and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Sections were subsequently incubated for 5 min in 0.1 M HCl and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Pre-hybridization was performed for 35 min as for RNA, then 5,000 ng of DNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution were added to sections and covered with coverglass. Sections were then incubated on a 90 °C hotplate for exactly 7 min and transferred to 42 °C overnight. The following morning, samples were washed twice in 2 × SSC for 10 min at 42 °C, once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then incubated in a post-fix solution (2% glutaraldehyde, 8% PFA in 1 × PBS) for 30 min. Samples were then washed three times in 2 × SSC and imaged.

Recent findings suggest that for ORCA experiments not involving RNA imaging, samples were fixed, permeabilized, cleared, treated with HCl, pre-hybridized and hybridized as described above, but omitting the protease step. Inclusion of the protease step was found to substantially improve RNA staining and was therefore used only for experiments that included RNA imaging. For ORCA experiments involving fluorescent protein labelling (for example, tdTomato signal in Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO), samples were first fixed and washed, imaged for the fluorescent protein and then processed for DNA ORCA as described above. Throughout all procedures, care was taken to prevent sections from drying at any point in the protocol to minimize tissue shrinkage between RNA or protein imaging rounds and subsequent DNA imaging rounds.

Industry observers note that samples hybridized with primary probes were imaged on a previously described custom microscopy and microfluidics setup29,52. RNA and DNA readout barcodes were labelled sequentially with a 750 dye complementary to the readout barcodes on primary probes. All RNA and DNA probes share a common sequence that was labelled with a Cy3 dye complementary to this sequence, referred to as the fiducial. Fiducial probes were added before the first imaging round and imaged alongside each barcode. Fiducial signal was subsequently used for drift correction and alignment across imaging rounds. For RNA imaging, the fiducial signal captures all stained RNAs, whereas for DNA imaging it appears as discrete puncta, with each punctum representing one Pcdh locus.

OE tissue was first stained for H3K9me3 as follows. Tissue on glass coverslips was fixed for 10 min in 4% PFA, washed twice in 1 × PBS, quenched for 5 min in PBS containing 0.1 M glycine and washed again in PBS. Tissue was permeabilized with three 5-min washes in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then blocked in PBS containing 1% BSA and 200 U ml−1 RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs, M0314L). Primary antibody incubation was performed overnight at 4 °C using rabbit anti-H3K9me3 antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Abcam, ab8898). The following morning, tissue was washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then incubated with donkey anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 647 secondary antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, A31573). Tissue was then washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100. Samples were stored at 4 °C in PBS protected from light until imaging. To image OE tissue with STORM, an imaging buffer was prepared immediately before use as follows. A dilution buffer was first prepared containing 50 mM NaCl and 200 mM Tris pH 8.0. A glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution was prepared by combining 700 μl of dilution buffer, 49 mg of glucose oxidase and 175 μl of catalase, centrifuging at maximum speed for 1 min and collecting 800 μl of supernatant. STORM imaging buffer was prepared by adding 800 μl of glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution, 8 ml of 50% glucose and 400 μl of β-mercaptoethanol to 32 ml of dilution buffer.

For each field of view, fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample immediately before imaging. H3K9me3 STORM videos were acquired at five axial positions using the 635-nm laser at maximum power and an exposure time of 0.5 s per frame. The first and fourth videos contained 3,000 frames, whereas the remaining videos contained 2,500 frames. Fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample after the third video to maintain fluorophore blinking during prolonged imaging. Further frames were acquired after addition of fresh buffer because extra illumination time was required for photobleaching before robust fluorophore blinking could be observed.

STORM videos were acquired across multiple axial planes rather than using astigmatism-based 3D STORM with a cylindrical lens53, because high tissue background made accurate fitting of astigmatic spot widths unreliable. The five axial planes were separated by 750 nm and sampled a 3.0-μm axial range centred on the plane with strongest H3K9me3 signal. Subsequent ORCA imaging of the same samples was acquired using Z-stacks containing matched axial planes to those imaged by STORM.

Fluorescently tagged WGA, which labels cell membranes, was used to align fields of view across imaging sessions (for example, to align H3K9me3 STORM, RNA and Pcdh DNA images). First, 3 μl of 1 ng μl−1 WGA was diluted in 600 μl of 2 × SSC, added to samples for 15 min, then washed off with 2 × SSC immediately before imaging. For RNA and Pcdh DNA imaging, the fiducial channel was imaged alongside the WGA signal at the end of each imaging session. For H3K9me3 STORM, WGA images for each field of view were taken immediately following completion of STORM acquisition. For imaging of fluorescent proteins tagging mOSNs, WGA was imaged simultaneously in a different channel alongside the fluorescent protein. When aligning images across RNA and DNA imaging rounds, images from each field of view were first aligned to the fiducial signal acquired with WGA, and fields of view were subsequently registered across imaging modalities using the WGA signal. The WGA signal additionally enabled 3D cell segmentation (described below).

All imaging was performed on a custom microscopy and microfluidics setup as previously described29,52. The details of the microscopy setup are also listed on the 4DN data portal and Mirco-Meta App54 under Stanford-Boettiger_lab_ORCA_Nikon_Eclipse_Ti2-U_Scope3.

Three-dimensional cell segmentations were generated from the WGA signal acquired during RNA imaging. We trained a Cellpose55 algorithm to identify cell outlines in individual sections of WGA images. This algorithm was then run on every section of WGA Z-stack images for each field of view. To connect the resulting two-dimensional (2D) cell segmentations into 3D cell segmentations, we applied ultrack56, an algorithm initially designed to track cells over time in time-series data, to the 2D segmentations for each stack, effectively treating the Z dimension as time. Ultrack produced 3D cell segmentations that matched WGA staining (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We used ultrack, as we found Cellpose’s performance with 2D images to be superior to its performance with 3D images for OE sections stained with WGA.

According to recent reports, segmented cells were classified into distinct cell types on the basis of RNA transcripts within each segmentation as follows. RNA puncta were first identified from 3D stacks using storm-analysis (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7679267), which identifies their X, Y position in each frame and is robust to overlapping spots. The Z position of each punctum was computed by fitting the axial fluorescence intensity profile to puncta with a common X, Y position (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7698979). RNA puncta were then mapped to cell segmentations and segmentations were classified by cell type as follows: for each cell, counts of Icam1, Ascl1, Tex15, Gap43 and Omp transcripts were log-transformed, Z-scored and combined into marker-specific scores corresponding to HBCs (Icam1), GBCs (Ascl1), INPs (Tex15), iOSNs (Gap43) and mOSNs (Omp high, Gap43 low). Cells were assigned to the cell type with the highest score, subject to further marker-based rules (Tex15+ cells were forced to INP and not allowed to be mOSN; HBC labels were forbidden in Gap43+ or Omp+ cells). A confidence score was defined as the difference between the top two scores, and cells with low confidence or ambiguous profiles were labelled ‘undetermined’. To map DNA loci to each segmentation, the X, Y, Z coordinates of DNA loci were transformed by the image alignments computed between WGA images. Each locus was then mapped to a classified cell from its respective field of view and assigned that cell’s label.

For ORCA experiments involving protein rather than RNA staining, DNA loci were classified as belonging to a particular cell type (namely, mOSNs) on the basis of the fluorescent signal of tdTomato. Apart from Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e, data in all figures come from cells classified as mOSNs.

After aligning images from RNA and DNA imaging rounds, the X, Y, Z positions of RNA puncta and DNA loci were registered into a common coordinate system. For each DNA locus, we computed the 3D Euclidean distance to every RNA punctum in the same field of view in voxel units, where X–Y coordinates are in pixels and Z is in imaging planes. A locus was classified as ‘transcribing’ for a given gene if at least one RNA punctum for that gene lay within a 3D distance of 8 voxel units, and as ‘non-transcribing’ otherwise. This threshold corresponds to 1.23–1.60 μm in physical space, depending on how the separation between DNA and RNA puncta is distributed across the X–Y and Z axes. The threshold of 8 voxel units was chosen on the basis of the distribution of nearest RNA distances across all DNA loci for each Pcdh RNA, which was consistently bimodal, with one population less than 8 voxel units and another greater than or equal to 8 voxel units.

It has been revealed that STORM videos were processed frame by frame using the 2dfixed multi-emitter-fitting algorithm from storm-analysis (https://github.com/ZhuangLab/storm-analysis). Initial frames dominated by saturated fluorescence before photobleaching were excluded. Single-molecule localizations in each frame were identified using a 10-sigma detection threshold and fit with a fixed-width 2D Gaussian model using an initial Gaussian sigma of 1.3 pixels. Drift correction was not applied during fitting. Localizations were fit independently for each axial imaging plane, and each localization was assigned the Z position of its corresponding imaging plane for downstream analysis.

Sources indicate that H3K9me3 STORM signal around Pcdh loci in mOSNs was quantified as the number of STORM localizations within a 324-nm radius, corresponding to 3 pixels, of the X–Y position of the fiducial signal of each locus. Similar results were obtained using different radius sizes. For each locus, localizations were counted from the STORM imaging plane or planes nearest to the locus in Z. If the locus was located in the same Z plane as a STORM video, only localizations from that plane were used. If the locus was located between two STORM imaging planes, localizations from both planes were included and linearly weighted according to their proximity to the locus Z position. For example, for a locus located at Z plane 26 between STORM videos acquired at planes 25 and 28, localizations from plane 25 were weighted by 2/3 and localizations from plane 28 were weighted by 1/3. For the analyses in Fig. 2f, the same quantification was performed using the X, Y and Z position of the ORCA barcode containing the Pcdh gene being analysed, rather than the fiducial position of the locus.

Industry observers note that for the simulations in Fig. 2c, randomized positions were used to compare H3K9me3 STORM signal at observed Pcdh loci with signal expected at other positions within the same nuclei. For each of 1,000 simulations, one random position was selected for each observed Pcdh locus from the same cell and Z plane, thereby controlling for non-uniform axial distribution of H3K9me3 STORM signal within individual cells. H3K9me3 STORM signal was quantified at each randomized position using the same 324-nm radius and Z-plane weighting scheme described above. The median STORM signal from each simulation was used to generate a null distribution, which was compared with the observed median STORM signal around Pcdh loci to calculate an empirical P value. The same randomization and quantification procedure was performed for putative Tex15 transcription sites in INPs for Extended Data Fig. 7d. Putative Tex15 transcription sites were identified from Tex15 RNA FISH z-stacks by detecting bright 3D regional maxima. For each field of view, the Tex15 stack was smoothed with a 3D Gaussian filter and thresholded to identify local maxima corresponding to candidate nascent RNA puncta. The intensity threshold was empirically chosen by visual inspection across fields of view to retain bright Tex15 transcription sites while excluding dimmer spots probably corresponding to mature transcripts.

Recent findings suggest that for visualization of H3K9me3 STORM localizations together with ORCA traces in three dimensions (Extended Data Fig. 7a), STORM localizations from each axial imaging plane were shown with a randomized Z position drawn from a truncated Gaussian distribution centred on the corresponding STORM imaging plane. The Gaussian had a standard deviation of 1.2 imaging-plane units and was truncated to ±3.5 imaging-plane units around the plane centre. This jittering was used only to create smooth 3D renderings of STORM signal across the sparsely sampled axial planes and was not used for quantitative analyses.

Image processing (drift correction and localization of spots) was performed as described previously29,52 using ORCA analysis tools (https://github.com/BoettigerLab/ORCA-public).

Before downstream analyses, ORCA traces were quality filtered on the basis of barcode detection. For each experiment, we computed the number of detected barcodes per trace. Median barcode detection per trace was calculated to be around 40–60 barcodes, and we restricted our analysis to traces with ≥25 detected barcodes. We further filtered out traces with unnaturally high barcode detection, keeping only traces with ≤86 barcodes detected. For each retained trace, the 3D positions of detected barcodes were ordered by genomic position. Next, barcodes with consistently poor detection or abnormal labelling (for example, failed strand displacement) were assigned estimated positions by linear interpolation in traces for which the immediately flanking barcodes were detected. This selective interpolation was applied to 2–5 barcodes per experiment. For contact frequency map analyses, such as those presented in Figs. 1e and 3e–g, we further interpolated missing barcodes using a maximum gap length of three consecutive missing barcodes. This interpolation preserved the major features of contact frequency maps while improving their smoothness. Different maximum gap lengths were tested. Gap lengths greater than three did not produce measurable further smoothing, whereas allowing larger interpolations produced abnormally short adjacent-barcode distances. For all other analyses, raw detected barcode positions were used, with only the selective interpolation of poorly labelled barcodes described above.

For contact frequency analyses, we chose contact thresholds near the average distance between adjacent barcodes in a spatially contiguous region of the locus. These thresholds ranged from 170 to 220 nm across experiments. We also conducted a threshold parameter sweep to verify that observed contact patterns were robust to a range of thresholds around the selected value, and varying the contact threshold within a reasonable range did not qualitatively alter any within-experiment effects. Thresholds were used to call contacts between all barcode pairs in an experiment. The thresholds used for each experiment are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

Enhancer–promoter barcode pairs were assigned on the basis of previously reported regulatory relationships between Pcdh cluster enhancers and their target promoters13,15,25,57, together with the ORCA locus positions containing the corresponding genes and enhancers. All Pcdha genes were assigned the HS5-1 enhancer (barcode 27), whereas Pcdhb genes were assigned the HS18-22 enhancer (barcode 78) and Pcdhg genes were assigned the HS16-17 enhancer (barcode 76). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies were extracted from contact frequency matrices generated from max-gap-3 interpolated polymer coordinates, as described above. For ORCA barcodes containing multiple Pcdh promoters, combined gene labels were used.

We defined the geometric centre of an ORCA trace as the median X, Y, Z position of all detected barcodes in that trace. For the distance-to-centre profiles in Fig. 1i, we computed the Euclidean distance between each barcode and this centre on a per-trace basis, then plotted, for each position, the median distance across all traces. When distances to the centre of the heterochromatin domain were measured in Fig. 4c and Extended Data Figs. 9a–d and 10d, the heterochromatin centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned to the heterochromatin domain (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67), and the distances of relevant locus positions to this centre were measured. When distances to the centre of a euchromatin region were measured in Extended Data Fig. 9a–d, the centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned either to the euchromatin stretch between the Pcdha and Pcdhb clusters (barcodes 15–28) or to the euchromatin stretch downstream of the Pcdhg cluster (barcodes 68–90), depending on the specific locus position being analysed.

Recent findings suggest that radius of gyration (\({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\)) was used as a single-number measure of the spatial spread of a set of barcodes around its geometric centre47. For a set of \(N\) barcodes with 3D coordinates {\({r}_{i}\)}, we first calculated the centre \(c\) as the coordinate-wise median position, then defined \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) as \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}{\sum }_{i=1}^{N}{||}{r}_{i}-c{{||}}^{2}}\). The \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) of the heterochromatin domain was primarily evaluated. In Fig. 5e, the heterochromatin domain \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) was calculated as a fraction of the trace-wide \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\).

Industry observers note that for each isoform measured in Fig. 4a, the promoter barcode was assigned on the basis of the ORCA locus position containing the respective Pcdh gene. The heterochromatin compartment was defined as barcodes 2–14 and 29–67. The euchromatin compartment was defined on the basis of the cluster of the promoter being analysed: barcodes 15–28 for Pcdha promoters, and barcodes 68–90 for Pcdhb and Pcdhg promoters. The promoter barcode itself was excluded from the compartment to which it belonged. For each trace, a promoter-to-heterochromatin centre distance was calculated as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all heterochromatin compartment barcodes. Promoter-to-euchromatin centre distances were calculated analogously as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all barcodes in the corresponding euchromatin compartment.

In a recent development, in Extended Data Fig. 10e, entropy was calculated for the distance distributions between pairs of locus positions as described previously58. For each barcode pair, we pooled 3D distances across all traces within each genotype separately, then normalized each genotype’s distances by that genotype’s own median distance for the pair to account for length-scale differences between experiments. We then pooled the normalized distances from both genotypes together and set common histogram bin edges (50 bins) using the 1st and 99th percentiles of this pooled, normalized distribution, so that entropy values were computed on the same scale for both genotypes. Using these shared bin edges, we separately estimated each genotype’s distribution, normalized bin counts to probabilities pk and computed Shannon entropy as \(S=-{\sum }_{k}{p}_{k}{\log }_{2}({p}_{k})\), such that higher S reflects broader, more variable distances and lower S indicates more narrowly peaked, reproducible distances. For each locus position, we calculated its entropy with respect to all other positions, averaged these pairwise entropies per position and compared the resulting mean entropies between Setdb1 cKO and WT.

Industry observers note that to quantify spatial segregation between heterochromatic and euchromatic regions of the Pcdh locus, we calculated a separation score as follows. For each polymer, we designated heterochromatin locus positions (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67) as region A and euchromatic locus positions (barcodes 15–28 and 68–90) as region B, computed all pairwise 3D distances and took the median distance between A and B (heterochromatin–euchromatin) and the median distance within A (heterochromatin–heterochromatin). The separation score was defined as the ratio of these two medians (medianA–B/medianA–A), such that higher values indicate that the heterochromatin domain is more spatially separated from neighbouring euchromatin. This score was computed per trace for WT, Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO and compared across genotypes.

To validate the specificity of RNA probes targeting Pcdha and Pcdhg isoforms, plasmids encoding Pcdha and Pcdhg variable exons fused to mCherry under control of a CMV promoter were generated through FastCloning59. Plasmid sequences were validated using Plasmidsaurus. Plasmids were transfected into Cath.a-differentiated cells grown in eight-well Ibidi glass-bottom plates (Ibidi, 80827). Cells were seeded at a density of 40,000 cells per well in 220 μl of media and transfected after 24 h of growth using lipofectamine (Invitrogen, L3000001). Each well was then stained with primary RNA probes according to the procedure described above. For 12 plasmids across each of the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, three wells were transfected, with each well stained by a different ORCA readout barcode. Only wells that were labelled with a readout barcode mapping to the Pcdh isoform they were transfected with produced signal.

Industry observers note that FACS isolation of mouse OSNs was performed as previously described15. In brief, mice were euthanized with CO2 followed by cervical dislocation and OE tissue was immediately dissected. Cells were then dissociated into a single-cell suspension by incubating freshly dissected tissue with papain for 30–40 min at 37 °C according to the Worthington Papain Dissociation System. After dissociation and filtering through a 35-μm cell strainer, cells were resuspended in 1 × PBS with 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS), DNase (0.0025% final concentration) and DAPI. Fluorescent cells were sorted on a FACS Aria Fusion cell sorter (BD Biosciences) with BD FACSDiva 9.0.1 software. Cells were sorted into 1 × PBS + 2% FBS. FACS gating strategies used to isolate GFP+ and tdTomato+ mOSNs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1.

scRNA-seq experiments were performed as previously described15. In brief, cells were dissociated from OE tissue from 4- to 5-week-old mice as described above. About 70,000 mOSNs were FACS-isolated. Complementary DNA and library preparation were performed using the 10x Genomics Single Cell 5′ Gene Expression workflow, and libraries were sequenced using a NovaSeq SP100 PE50 and a NextSeq 2000 P2 200 through the UCSF Gladstone Genomic Core and the UCSF Center for Advanced Technology. Sequencing data were processed using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger 6.0.1. Data analysis was performed using Seurat60,61 and custom scripts. Cells were filtered to retain cells with 1,000–10,000 detected genes and less than 5% mitochondrial reads. Counts were then normalized using Seurat’s NormalizeData with log normalization and a scale factor of 10,000. See Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 for further details on scRNA-seq analysis and statistics.

According to recent reports, for analyses in Fig. 5 and Extended Data Fig. 10, Pcdh isoform choice was analysed in mOSNs defined by detected Omp expression and no detected Gap43 expression using raw unique molecular identifier counts. A Pcdh isoform was considered detected in a given mOSN if one or more unique molecular identifier-corrected reads were assigned to that gene. For each condition, the percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh isoform was calculated as the fraction of mOSNs with detected expression of that isoform. Changes in Pcdh choice across genotypes were calculated as percentage-point differences relative to WT. Data for single-cell experiments represent one biological replicate per condition.

Industry observers note that nChIP–seq was performed as previously described62. Briefly, live cells were sorted from papain-dissociated mouse OE; in experiments for which spike-ins were included to enable quantification of ChIP signal across conditions, HEK293T cells at around 70% confluency were trypsinized, washed with PBS and added at a ratio of 0.75% to the sorted mouse cells. (HEK293T cells were grown in RPMI or DMEM media supplemented with 10% FBS and 1 × penicillin-streptomycin, incubated at 37 °C and 5% CO2, and tested for mycoplasma (ATCC Universal Mycoplasma Detection Kit) before use in experiments.) Live sorted cells were pelleted in a swinging bucket centrifuge (800g, 15 min, 4 °C) and then resuspended in Buffer 1 (0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Cells were lysed on ice for 10 min by adding an equal volume of Buffer 2 (0.4% Igepal CA-630, 0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Nuclei were pelleted (1,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in MNase buffer (0.32 M sucrose, 4 mM MgCl2, 1 mM CaCl2, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Resuspended nuclei were treated with MNase (Sigma) at 37 °C, and the reaction was quenched with the addition of EDTA to a final concentration of 20 mM. Two fractions of solubilized chromatin were collected; nuclei were pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S1 was collected and stored at 4 °C overnight. Nuclei were resuspended in Dialysis Buffer (1 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors) and rotated overnight at 4 °C. Insoluble material was pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S2 was retained. MNase treatment was optimized to yield predominantly mono-nucleosomes in the S1 fraction and predominantly di-nucleosomes, tri-nucleosomes and some larger chromatin fragments in the S2 fraction. S1 and S2 DNA concentrations were measured by HS DNA Qubit after RNase A treatment. Equal volumes of S1 and S2 fractions were pooled, and total yields were estimated. In spike-in experiments, chromatin input was not always equalized across immunoprecipitations, as spike-in normalization accounts for differences in input.

MNase-digested chromatin was diluted in Wash Buffer 1 (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 10 mM EDTA, 125 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and 5% inputs were reserved. Histone H3 lysine 9 tri-methyl antibody (H3K9me3, Abcam ab8898) was added, and the binding reaction was rotated overnight at 4 °C. For each immunoprecipitation, 20 μl of Dynabeads Protein G (Invitrogen) were blocked overnight with 2 mg ml−1 yeast transfer RNA and 2 mg ml−1 BSA in Wash Buffer 1. The next day, blocked beads were added to antibody-bound chromatin and rotated for 1–3 h at 4 °C. Chromatin-bound beads were washed at 4 °C a total of four times with Wash Buffer I, three times with Wash Buffer II (5 mM Tris pH 7.5, 17.5 mM NaCl, 0.01% NP-40, 1 mM EDTA, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and one time with Tris-EDTA buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 mM EDTA). Two 15-min elutions were conducted at 37 °C in Elution Buffer (1% SDS, 250 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT). ChIP DNA and input DNA were column purified using Zymo ChIP DNA columns (Zymo Research, D5205 or D5201).

Libraries were prepared using the Ovation Ultralow V2 DNA-Seq Library Preparation Kit (Tecan Life Sciences). The quality of the libraries was assessed by Bioanalyzer and quantified using a combination of Bioanalyzer and Qubit. Libraries were pooled and sequenced on a NextSeq 2000 (Gladstone Institutes), NextSeq 500/550 (UCSF Center for Advanced Technology) or NovaSeq X (Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Biohub San Francisco).

Data processing and analysis was conducted in accordance with previous literature63,64. For spike-in experiments, adapters were trimmed with cutadapt with --minimum-length 18 and checked for sequencing quality control with FastQC. Reads were aligned with Bowtie2 to a concatenated mouse and human genome (mm10 + hg38) in which the spike-in chromosomes were pre-labelled with a ‘_hg38’ suffix. Alignments were split by chromosome using bamUtil’s splitChromosome function, and samtools’ merge command was used to collect mouse and human alignments separately. Then, duplicates were marked and removed using Picard MarkDuplicates, and the spike-in chromosome suffix was stripped. Alignments with mapping quality < 30 were removed using samtools, and read counts aligning to the mouse and human genomes were used to calculate spike-in scaling factors.

It has been revealed that as in the original ChIP-Rx method describing quantitative spike-in normalized ChIP followed by sequencing, our spike-in corrections normalized for the number of spike-in reads in the immunoprecipitation63. We sequenced every input as well, allowing us to adjust for the variability in spike-in read fraction in each input64,65. The spike-in adjusted coverage signal, \({z}_{i}\), was calculated from counts per million (CPM)-normalized coverage values, \({x}_{i}\), with the equation \({z}_{i}={x}_{i}\cdot \frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), where \({S}_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{in}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the inputs, respectively, and \({S}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the immunoprecipitations, respectively. Bigwig files were generated from Deeptools bamCoverage using --scaleFactor of \(\frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\cdot \frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), --binSize 10, --minMappingQuality 30 and --normalizeUsing CPM. In Fig. 5c, to compare spike-in-normalized nChIP–seq values from different experiments, we batch-corrected using the average of the scale factors from the WT samples within each experimental batch. Significance was assessed and confirmed using both a Welch’s unpaired t-test and a two-way ANOVA (main effects only).

It has been revealed that for experiments without spike-ins, adapters were trimmed and the first 4 nucleotides of each read removed with cutadapt (v1.9.1; -u 4, --minimum-length 18). Reads were aligned to mm10 with Bowtie2. BigWig files were generated with deepTools bamCoverage in 10-base-pair bins from unextended reads, normalized to 1 × genome coverage (reads per genomic content; effective genome size 2,407,883,318; chr. X, chr. Y and chr. M excluded from normalization).

Immunohistochemistry for RAD21 was performed as described previously15. A similar staining protocol was performed for SETDB1, with minor modifications to the blocking buffer composition to improve signal. Sections were removed from −20 °C, washed in 1 × PBS for 5 min at room temperature, then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min. Sections were incubated in blocking solution (3% BSA, 0.2% Tween in 4 × SSC) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibody incubation proceeded overnight (12–16 h) at 4 °C in a humidified chamber. The following morning, sections were washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature, then incubated in secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Samples were then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature and mounted under coverslips with antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories, H-2000-2). For RAD21 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:100 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, PA5-28344). For SETDB1 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:250 in blocking buffer (Thermofisher, MA5-47120). For both RAD21 and SETDB1, secondary antibody was added at 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen donkey anti-rabbit 647, A31573).

The Hi-C data in Extended Data Fig. 2b and bulk RNA-seq data in Fig. 3b were previously published and re-analysed as described15.

(k) Model of Pcdh transcription from a megabase-scale heterochromatin domain. Pcdh enhancers lie outside the heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh promoters. Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion brings enhancers into the domain to engage promoters, with transcription initiating from within the domain. After promoter activation, transcription can proceed in the absence of enhancer—promoter engagement. Transcription reads through downstream Pcdha and Pcdhg genes residing within the heterochromatin domain, and domain-scale compaction is maintained.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It wasn’t Hercules, but Matias Soulé who lit up the Parc des Princes.

The Argentine talent took just five minutes to become the star of yet another great European night: a decisive assist for Hermoso after dancing to the ball, skipping past opponents.

It has been revealed that gian Piero Gasperini expressed his satisfaction at seeing a player continually improving: “Besides being strong, he’s very positive, he’s receptive, and he wants to grow. He’s 23, and he’s in a period where he can grow, as he is doing. He’s more complete than before; today he’s played on the left, whereas until last year he was stuck on that pitch. He’s reaching extraordinary technical and physical maturity. I’m happy for him; in these last two months, he’s been doing something very positive.”.

Matias Soulé demonstrates no signs of slowing down his unstoppable growth. The Argentine winger has already been involved in 10 goals this season, one every 114 minutes: four goals and six assists in 17 appearances.

The Argentine talent’s performances this year are rising in proportion to the quality of his opponents: he has rarely been without a hand in big matches.

In fact, Soulé scored one goal and provided three assists in the Champions League matches against Real Madrid, Manchester United, and PSG.

Sources indicate that in the league, he was instrumental with a goal that allowed Roma to a last-gasp 2-1 victory against Atalanta, adding to his assist for Hermoso that temporarily tied the game 1-1. On October 24, he lit up the Maradona stadium with a total performance from start to finish, further enhanced by the goal that sparked the comeback to secure a 3-3 draw at Napoli.

Gasperini’s Roma earns the respect of the football world.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Heaton’s smile mentioned a lot about Manchester United’s decision to do post-match weight training on the side of the pitch and in the view of the media.
  • Manchester United drew 2-2 away at Sporting in a game filled with incident.
  • A lot of the talk surrounding Pochettino’s arrival at Old Trafford is that the players better be ready to work hard and so what better way to demonstrate that work than by having the players perform a weight routine on the side of the pitch where all the cameras can see them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Heaton’s smile mentioned a lot about Manchester United’s decision to do post-match weight training on the side of the pitch and in the view of the media.

Manchester United drew 2-2 away at Sporting in a game filled with incident. Three penalties, one red card, a goalkeeper howler and a horrendous pitch-enforced bobble means that Mauricio Pochettino will have to wait until his third game at least for his first win in charge.

A lot of the talk surrounding Pochettino’s arrival at Old Trafford is that the players better be ready to work hard and so what better way to demonstrate that work than by having the players perform a weight routine on the side of the pitch where all the cameras can see them.

The TNT cameras were on hand to capture the United players doing weight routines on the side of the pitch with Shea Lacey front and centre.

One player who looked slightly bemused as to why this was happening is third-choice goalkeeper Tom Heaton.

The 40-year-old, who has been around the block a few times, gave a cheeky look towards the cameras as if to say “yes, we are doing performative weight training on the side of the pitch.”.

All of this is part of Project Pochettino which aims to turn the unbothered United squad into one of the hardest-working in the Premier League.

But he will want to start winning games as soon as possible and suggested they should have on Wednesday night.

“I think we dominated and we deserved to win the game, but we didn’t for different circumstances,” he said.

“All the teams make mistakes, but for these mistakes the punishment is too massive in every single mistake. Many other clubs make mistakes or tilt in a different circumstance, in a more positive way. But that is in the way we are. We need to take responsibility.”.

READ: The 11 Man Utd players out on loan in 2026-27 & how they’ve been faring.

Pochettino may also have a problem in goal after Senne Lammens, who at one point in his United career looked like a much-needed safe pair of hands, spilt an easy catch for Sporting’s second.

Pochettino, though, defended his player and said these things happen.

According to recent reports, “This type of thing happens,” he said. “That is football. Football is about making mistakes.

“I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.

“It’s not to blame the defensive line, but it’s two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage this type of situation better.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nuno Mendes acknowledged the difficulties Paris Saint-Germain faced in their 2-2 draw against Roma at the Parc des Princes.

The Portuguese full-back, playing in the mixed zone, praised the tactical work of Gian Piero Gasperini’s team, which caused considerable difficulty for the French and European champions with intense pressing and precise organization.

“There are teams that will try to play this way in the future, and we’ll be ready. We already know what we have to do for the full 90 minutes. They caused our team a lot of problems, but I think we managed to overcome their pressure at times.”.

In a recent development, “There were also moments when they managed to find space, win the ball back, and cause us problems. They were one of the most difficult teams to face. We have our own way of playing, and we never change. They analyzed it carefully, just as we had studied Roma, but they still managed to create a lot of problems for us. There are games where we can’t always be at our best, but we’ll keep trying.”.
