📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The controversy surrounding Jamal Musiala is far from falling on Bayern Munich. For several days, the Bavarian management’s comments on the future of the attacking midfielder and his imposing salary have sparked a wave of indignation in Germany. After Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, it is now Maik Franz who has stepped up to the plate. Guest of the show Doppelpass on Sport1the former defender did not mince his words to denounce the attitude of the Munich board, which he considers particularly inappropriate towards a player facing health problems. At the heart of this controversy, the statements of Rummenigge, who publicly questioned Musiala’s salary conditions in view of his physical difficulties and his level of performance.

According to recent reports, an outing which provoked numerous reactions, notably from Maik Franz: “what the Bayern leaders are doing, and I’m not talking about Kompany and Eberl, who are behaving in an exemplary manner, but about MM. Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge, is pathetic and even, in my eyes, constitutes harassment. We can discuss a player’s performance. But it is not appropriate to talk publicly about an illness and the salary associated with it, at this level. We must not forget that Jamal tried everything to come back. He highlighted a lot of courage and transparency in discussing his diagnosis. For this to turn against him today is not acceptable. To be completely honest, we are no longer in “Mia san Mia”, but in “Mia san money”. Money takes precedence over people. And this must not happen.”.

The controversy even went beyond the borders of Bavarian management to affect the locker room. Michael Olise actually liked an Instagram post from Fabrizio Romano relaying the press release from FIFPRO, the international players’ union, which called on Bayern to respect Jamal Musiala. A particularly notable gesture from the French international, renowned for his discretion on social networks. This support takes on an additional dimension as Bayern wish to extend Olise’s contract, at the moment linked to the club until 2029. Maik Franz also underlined the risk that this affair could represent for decision-makers: “With Michael Olise, you may have the next best player in the world in your ranks. He too must extend and receive a substantial salary. But you keep in mind that if you got sick or injured and didn’t perform, you would be publicly thrown out to waste. Frankly, I don’t think they did themselves any favors.”.

FIFPRO also strongly criticized Bayern’s communication, saying contractual issues should be discussed privately with the player and his representatives. The union notably recalled that an injury or decline in form did not justify publicly calling into question salary conditions already agreed upon. While Musiala tries to regain his best level after a long period of absence, the Bavarian club finds itself under fire from critics. Between the declarations of its leaders, the exit of Maik Franz and the remarkable gesture of Olise, the file has become a real image concern for Bayern Munich….

The story of Eric Cantona and his incredible impact on Man Utd

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Planetfootball

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on May 17, 1997, Eric Cantona announced his retirement from football.
  • That was one of the more extreme responses from a supporter outside Old Trafford (see video below) the day after Cantona stunned football – not for the first time and certainly not for the last – by signing for Manchester United.
  • As a 12-year-old red growing up in a Leeds United heartland, I certainly wasn’t sure how to process the breaking story late in the Calendar News bulletin at 6.25pm on Thursday, November 26, 1992.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on May 17, 1997, Eric Cantona announced his retirement from football. He was only 30 years old, but his impact on Manchester United and on English football had been immeasurable.

“‘Ooh ahh, Cantona’? They won’t sing it here.”.

That was one of the more extreme responses from a supporter outside Old Trafford (see video below) the day after Cantona stunned football – not for the first time and certainly not for the last – by signing for Manchester United.

As a 12-year-old red growing up in a Leeds United heartland, I certainly wasn’t sure how to process the breaking story late in the Calendar News bulletin at 6.25pm on Thursday, November 26, 1992.

According to recent reports, cantona had played a significant part in my misery up to that point, and his chant had provided the backing music for some merciless stick at school six months earlier when he helped Leeds deny my team their first Championship in 25 years. Yet here he was, switching sides.

Alex Ferguson did little to reassure his club’s supporters that there was method to the madness when he admitted Cantona only came into his mind “more or less” when Leeds called to enquire about Denis Irwin.

Cantona had only joined Leeds in January, signed for £900,000 by Howard Wilkinson from Nimes, and though the then-24-year-old made only six starts and another nine appearances off the bench in the second half of that 1991-92 season, his cameos helped Leeds beat Ferguson’s men to the title.

Cantona’s three goals came at home against teams in the lower half of the table, but he got the ball rolling against Luton and Wimbledon and broke Chelsea’s resistance with one of the goals of the season.

With Cantona, Leeds took 13 points from their final five games of the run-in, while Man Utd drew one and lost three on the spin against Nottingham Forest, West Ham and Liverpool to almost gift-wrap the final pre-Premier League title for their Yorkshire rivals.

Though Ferguson acknowledged in both autobiographies that Leeds were worthy champions, his side unquestionably blew it as his fear over the goals drying up became a reality.

In a recent development, coincidence though it may be, when Leeds signed Cantona, Man Utd were averaging 2.9 goals per game over 26 matches. In the final 16-game run-in, that plummeted to one goal per game, while they were shut out six times.

Sixteen games into the following campaign, United were eighth and again averaging only a goal per game when a call took place which changed the face of English football.

“I remember that phone call clearly, as though it was yesterday,” Leeds’ former Managing director Bill Fotherby stated in 2012.

It has been revealed that “We agreed to pay Eric something like £500,000 if we kept him after the initial period of six months. It was an immense amount of money for Leeds, but we agreed to it because we had this recommendation from Michel Platini and we judged the most vital thing was to get the player.

Industry observers note that “We wanted to do whatever it took and deal with the rest afterwards. But there were difficulties almost immediately.

It has been revealed that “Apart from Lee Chapman, no-one in the squad spoke fluent French, and for Howard, it was a bit of a nightmare. Although we had won the title, there was just no connection between the two and, in the end, he told me to try and find Eric another club.

According to recent reports, “Howard Wilkinson was an absolute perfectionist. He wanted his players to be disciplined and adhere to a certain team pattern. Eric just didn’t fit it.

While Cantona might not have been suited to Leeds, he found his perfect match across the Pennines.

“If ever there was one player, anywhere in the word, that was made for Manchester United, it was Cantona,” said Ferguson later.

It has been revealed that “He swaggered in, stuck his chest out, raised his head and surveyed everything as though he were asking: ‘I’m Cantona. How big are you? Are you big enough for me?’”.

Ince, the self-styled Guvnor, remarked Cantona “took the responsibility away from us lot”, which was evident from the manner in which United attacked the second half of the season.

They doubled their goals per game over the remaining 26 matches, netting 50 times in 18 wins, losing only twice on their way to breaking a 26-year title drought. Famine was about to become feast.

It has been revealed that ferguson had been searching for a goalscorer, but in Cantona he found something rarer. The Frenchman notched nine goals over the remainder of the season, perhaps not a Shearer-esque strike-rate, but he offered 11 assists.

More than anything tangible, Cantona brought a swagger and a confidence which often strutted over the border to an arrogance that so inspired his team-mates and wowed fans at the now Stretford End-less Old Trafford.

Industry observers note that with Bryan Robson’s powers waning, Cantona arrived at the perfect time. Countless team-mates have referenced how the Frenchman became the example to follow at The Cliff. They had a latest leader.

Even Ferguson admits Cantona “opened my eyes to the indispensability of practice”.

It has been revealed that with Cantona leading the line, United felt and often looked invincible. The burden of responsibility Ince referred to was gone, and they followed up the title in 1993 with their first-ever Double in 1994.

Cantona, with his collar up, was at the heart of all that the purists identified as good and bad about that 93-94 team. He scored 25 goals in all competitions and contributed 13 assists, earning himself the PFA Player of the Year award.

There was no sign of the temper United had been warned about until the Champions League trip to Galatasaray in November 1993 when Cantona received his first red card in a United shirt for insulting the referee, who he later accused of being “bought”.

As he and his team-mates descended down the steps towards the underground changing rooms, Cantona was slyly attacked by a baton and shield-wielding policeman, as was Robson when the skipper rushed to defend his team-mate.

“In the dressing room, Eric went crazy,” Roy Keane recalled in his autobiography. “While the rest of us just wanted to get out of there, Eric was determined to sort out the rogue cop who had been wielding his truncheon.

In a recent development, “Eric was a substantial, strong lad. He was serious. He insisted he was going to kill that f***er. It took the combined efforts of the manager, Brian Kidd and a few of the players to restrain him.”.

Much like supporters, Cantona’s blood boiled at the thought of any perceived injustice, and that connection made it easy for United fans to not only forgive Eric’s misdemeanours but to revel in them.

In a recent development, cantona simmered over later that season when he was banned for five games after red cards in successive draws at Swindon and Arsenal. But those incidents were merely child’s play compared to what was to come at Crystal Palace the following season.

The kung-fu kick on Matthew Simmons was the release of 48 minutes of frustration after Cantona had felt he had been kicked around Selhurst Park without any protection from Alan Wilkie.

Cantona questioned the referee at half-time while, according to Wilkie, Ferguson was more direct: “Why don’t you do your f*cking job!”.

Three minutes after emerging from the tunnel for the second half, Cantona was being directed back towards it after dishing out his own form of justice to his shadow for the night, Richard Shaw.

We all know what happened next.

According to recent reports, ferguson indicates he has “never been able to elicit an explanation from Eric” as to why he felt the need to react to Matthew Simmons that way. Unsurprisingly, it seems he did it because he felt like it.

“Millions of times people say these things, and then one day you don’t accept it,” Cantona mentioned.

Sources indicate that “Why? It’s not about words. It’s about how you feel at that moment. One day you react, but the words are exactly the same as those you have heard a million times, so it is impossible to say why you react.”.

Cantona was subsequently suspended for nine months by the FA, and United went on to miss out on the title by a single point to Blackburn before losing the FA Cup final to Everton a week later.

To make matters worse, the FA threatened to extend Cantona’s suspension because he had been photographed taking part in a friendly against Rochdale that was nothing more than a behind-closed-doors kickabout of three thirds.

Cantona reacted by submitting a transfer request in early August.

Inter Milan, who were at Selhurst Park on that night in January to scout Cantona, would have been delighted to offer him a haven in Italy, but Ferguson travelled to Paris to convince his star player to stay put.

He later described that journey as “one of the more worthwhile acts I have performed in this stupid job of mine”.

Recent findings suggest that given the success that followed, that must rate as one of Ferguson’s greatest understatements. Another Double, this time with kids, and an additional Premier League title after that certainly justified his decision to smooth the path back for Cantona.

Cantona’s critics question his record, especially in European competition – though a goal every other game over six seasons and an assist for every three of his 185 appearances certainly stands up to scrutiny.

But Cantona’s contribution cannot be assessed by numbers.

United fans remember the moments. The good ones were incredible, and even the bad ones were great.

Notable goals, like the volley at Newcastle to break Kevin Keegan’s heart or the retreating shot from the edge of the box to win the 1996 FA Cup final against Liverpool’s Spice Boys.

And great goals too, against Sunderland or an even better lob in a gale at Sheffield United.

It has been revealed that eric Cantona vs Sheffield United, 1995. pic.twitter.com/CukcNEykQm.

— 90s Football (@90sfootball) June 27, 2020.

In terms of technique, Cantona was the best Old Trafford had seen for some time, but with regard to charisma, he was perhaps the greatest ever.

Robson will always be revered – despite not being a United product, he was the Stretford End’s representative on the pitch. Work hard, play hard, tackle harder, Captain Marvel was easy to relate to, but Eric was an enigma as well as an icon.

Never misunderstood at Old Trafford but being barely understood by his public certainly added to the mercurial Frenchman’s charm.

Like many of us were told about Best, Law and Charlton, there is now a generation of supporters who were never lucky enough to experience Cantona first-hand, and no amount of YouTube highlights videos can make those poor souls feel what Eric made United fans feel in the 1990s.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.
  • Sources indicate that in Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame.
  • Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that promptly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

Sources indicate that in Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that promptly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange new worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!".

Recent findings suggest that stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Firm, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in New York.

Recent findings suggest that in the same year,  Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a fresh edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation.".

According to recent reports, the successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a significant deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway.".

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

It has been revealed that in 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to issues such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the Newly introduced York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”.

Recent findings suggest that kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”.

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Recent findings suggest that kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and mentioned: “You held it together. You got through it.” It revealed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

It has been revealed that kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg.

Sources indicate that for his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Industry observers note that kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

In a recent development, both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he mentioned. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Industry observers note that kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

In a recent development, and he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and mentioned he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

According to recent reports, for the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

According to recent reports, kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN.

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

Sources indicate that first up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany remarked: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”.

It has been revealed that the plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has unveiled Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before promptly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

It has been revealed that the 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Industry observers note that kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Industry observers note that last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Industry observers note that selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

According to recent reports, in total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

The official ceremony begins at 8pm GMT.

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 13:00 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 13:13 EST, 25 November 2026.

Nicky Devlin has predicted that Findlay Marshall will continue to sparkle if he’s played at the top of Aberdeen’s diamond formation.

On the back of netting his first senior goal for the Dons from the bench against Kilmarnock, upcoming boss Mario Frick deployed the 20-year-old from the start against Rangers in a central attacking role.

In what proved to be a man of the match display, Marshall set up Brad Lyons’ opener then claimed a goal of his own with a sweet left-foot finish.

And with Frick seemingly intent on sticking with the blueprint which caused Killie and Rangers problems, defender Devlin believes his younger team-mate, who enjoyed a successful loan spell at Arbroath last season, will only go from strength to strength.

‘Even at Arbroath, you saw how much of a goal threat he is,’ mentioned Devlin. ‘He makes really good runs into the box and off both feet he’s a really good finisher.

Sources indicate that ‘He can definitely play other roles, especially in the formation that the manager’s been playing just now. But I think you get the best out of him when you let him attack the box, let him get into the box to score goals.

‘For me, he was the best player on the park. Especially for someone so young, to go there... he’ll probably hate me for saying it, but I could tell he was maybe a wee bit nervous because he told me about three or four times that it’s the first time he’d ever been to Ibrox.

Findlay Marshall in the thick of the action against Rangers in this week's 3-2 loss for Dons.

Industry observers note that ‘So, I knew he was thinking about it. But then he goes and delivers a performance like that.

‘His finishing, especially off his left foot, is unbelievable. He could easily have got us a draw. He was really unlucky with an effort right at the end.

It has been revealed that ‘He’s grown so much, especially since I came to the club at first. He’s an example for everyone at our club in terms of youth players. He’s gone and done what the club wanted him to do. He’s had two or three different loans where he’s gone away, played well, scored goals, came back, had to wait his opportunity.

‘In the last two games that he’s come in, he’s scored two goals and he’s been brilliant.’.

Marshall’s first goal for the Dons at Rugby Park was another crisp left-foot finish which came when he decided not to play in a team-mate.

Devlin feels that the better decision-making he’s now showing is a sign that his game is starting to click into place.

Industry observers note that ‘He’s a younger boy who just wants to learn all the time,’ he explained. ‘He mentioned after the game on Saturday that he had a chance like that in the cup and he chose the other option. He tried to play in maybe the more senior player just because he thought that was the right thing to do. He took on board that he should have maybe gone himself.

In a recent development, ‘It was an unbelievable finish. That’s what he brings to the team. That’s what he can bring to us. And hopefully he can keep doing that.’.

Marshall is only 20 but was Aberdeen's star man in the match at Ibrox on Tuesday night.

Born in Stonehaven and part of the Dons’ set-up since 2017, Marshall is the fresh poster boy for the club.

At a time when the opportunities being afforded to young Scots is a hot topic, Devlin feels that Aberdeen have much to feel optimistic about on that score.

‘I think we’ve got plenty here that I think can definitely step up and come in,’ he explained.

Recent findings suggest that ‘You see towards the end of the game, we’re chasing a goal with 20 minutes to go and the manager turns to a 15-year-old (Andrew Fasanya). So, there’s players there that can come through.

‘There’s a few boys out on loan now that are doing excellent. The two Alfies at Inverness (Bavidge and Stewart) and Dylan Lobban has done brilliant at Dunfermline.

Until the glory of World Cup 2018, I’d only ever seen England win one penalty shootout and it was thanks to the moustachioed ‘safe hands’ David Seaman.

#129002. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

📅 30 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1178 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships.
  • Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.
  • It has been revealed that the dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

It has been revealed that the dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

Industry observers note that the plate and the photos are on show at the upcoming exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, notes exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

According to recent reports, alongside Picasso, a surprising number of crucial artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to concern a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

It has been revealed that still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

In a recent development, however, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous.".

According to recent reports, the endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian notes. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character.".

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

Recent findings suggest that the designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany.".

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

It has been revealed that the feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really.".

  • Here’s an XI of players who supported the club in their youth that are better than the current XI turning out for the club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United‘s worldwide appeal, especially in the early 2000s, means there are plenty of current footballers who were fans of the club in their childhood.

Teams that are 19th in the Premier League don’t tend to have massive fanbases, but welcome to the contradiction that is modern Manchester United.

Here’s an XI of players who supported the club in their youth that are better than the current XI turning out for the club.

Considering some of the keepers United have had in recent years, how they could have used Courtois.

The Belgian keeper, who has become one of the very best, grew up a United fan due to Edwin van der Sar.

In a recent development, “I loved Edwin van der Sar and Casillas,” he told Rio Ferdinand. “So Casillas was because of his young age when he came into the goal at Madrid.

“At my age, I think I was like 12 or 11 at that time. Like I was just starting being goalkeeper. I really also blew my mind. Like, wow, he’s in Real Madrid.

“And I always followed those games. And then I followed always Manchester United for Edwin.”.

He even revealed that he was close to joining United before they signed David de Gea.

Now at Lille, Thomas Meunier has long been pinning his colours to the United mast.

In 2017, he said: “I’m a massive fan of Manchester United, which remains, in my eyes, the real reference in the world of football.”.

And even recently, he remarked he would cycle to Manchester if given the opportunity.

Industry observers note that “If they ever ask me, I’ll cycle there. But maybe it’s better this way. Suppose I play there and have a bad time. I wouldn’t want to hate Manchester United, because I love that club so much.

Akanji noted he is “no longer” a United fan after he joined City but sorry Manuel, the internet has receipts.

He told German newspaper NZZ that he had been a United fan “since my childhood days.”.

He swiftly stopped talking about that since he signed for their city rivals, though.

Dier never outright remarked he was a United fan, but there are certainly signs.

Mainly, it was who he listed as his idols during an interview with the Players’ Tribune.

“I was a big fan of Roy Keane when I was younger, and then it was Nemanja Vidic (one of the reasons I like the number 15 is Vidic) and his defensive partner, Rio Ferdinand.”.

He played a crucial part in City’s most successful ever period* but he was actually a United fan.

Stones has never outright remarked he grew up a United fan, maybe because the idea of Yorkshiremen doing so is a big no-no, but there is plenty of speculation online that he did indeed support the club.

Before he headed to Brighton, Caicedo named the two clubs in world football he would love to play for.

“In the short term: perform well and get Beerschot out of this plight. And in the long term? I am a fan of Manchester United and Real Madrid. It would be great to play there someday,” he told Gazet van Antwerpen.

A £100 million move to Chelsea has killed that dream for now but it would not be completely out of the question for him one day to be at Old Trafford.

Maddison’s support for United was spearheaded by David Beckham, who was playing for the Old Trafford side when Maddison was at the peak age when kids get drawn into football.

“In my early football days, I was a Manchester United fan and [Beckham] was at the forefront of that,” Maddison told talkSPORT.

“He was the guy on the back of my shirt, I went into the garden practising his free-kicks. The amount of times in school lessons I’d be watching David Beckham free-kicks on YouTube, it was silly really.”.

How United could do with Beckham or Maddison now.

Palmer is just about the most famous Manchester United fan playing right now.

There is a picture often circulated online of Palmer as a boy wearing the 2010-11 home kit and in 2024, he confirmed he was a fan of the club as a child.

That fandom has him linked to United every transfer window.

Gibbs-White is another player to tell Rio Ferdinand that he was a United fan.

Speaking on the former United centre-back’s podcast, Gibbs-White picked out Rooney and Scholes as the players he most enjoyed watching.

“Growing up as a kid, I supported Man Utd. [Wayne] Rooney was always my favourite player. He was the key player in that squad. Another player I loved watching was Paul Scholes, he used to just pick the ball up and zing it everywhere.”.

This one is a bit of rumour, but Nicky Butt claims that current Liverpool star Ngumoha was actually a United fan.

“I think he was at 13 or 14 or whatever age it was, he goes and looks around Man Utd – whether it be Old Trafford or Carrington,” Butt remarked on his podcast.

It has been revealed that “He’s gone with his family to look around the football club, and then he’s gone to Liverpool. And he’s picked Liverpool, and he’s a Man Utd fan.

“He should not be allowed out of that building before he signed that contract. It would never have happened.”.

Since signing for Liverpool, Ngumoha has clearly been told to never mention the United fandom thing.

Scoring in six consecutive matches has clearly made Evanilson confident he could fit in at a Major Six club and he has alerted United to the fact he is a big fan.

Evanilson told Globo Esporte: “So I joke around with Rayan. I think that, here in England, of the big clubs, United are the team I like the most. Rayan said the same thing. When I was a kid, I also used to watch United.

“When Cristiano Ronaldo played for United, I watched loads of his highlights. And, man, knowing that I’m here playing against them….

“It’s a dream, and I tell everyone this in interviews: it was a dream to play at that stadium, and scoring goals is even more vital.

“So it’s a dream I’ve been fulfilling, scoring a goal against United because of how big the club is.”.

There’s a come-and-get-me plea.

Mourinho arrived in west London in the summer of 2004, declaring himself the Special One and quickly building a title-winning side.

The Blues swept all before them in 2005 and 2006, before Mourinho departed in September 2007 having fallen out with Roman Abramovich.

Happily, he returned to Chelsea six years later and won a further Premier League title in 2015.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Punditry work is the lucrative alternative to management for retired ex-footballers and some earn more than a pretty penny for their time.

TV companies want ex-pros to front their coverage and for some audiences, watching the after-match debate has become as entertaining as watching the actual football.

As was the case when they were playing, the best ones get paid the massive bucks but who are the biggest earners in football?

Industry observers note that we’ve done our best to put together an accurate list but it is worth noting a couple of things. First off, the BBC’s Royal Charter means that they have to declare anyone who receives over £178k so anyone earning below that will not feature in this list.

Another important point to note is that the salaries of TNT pundits like Peter Crouch and Joe Cole are far more secretive than those at Sky.

But with those caveats in mind, here are the top earners in the UK.

Scott is the closest thing we have to Gary Lineker now that the former Match of the Day host has left in that player-turned-pundit-turned-presenter mould.

She has worked with the BBC since 2017, covering her first tournament at the 2018 World Cup, but was not picked as one of the hosts of Match of the Day.

Instead, she has branched out away from sport and also presents The One Show.

Some reports have Redknapp’s salary as high as £750k a year but that seems a little unrealistic.

Redknapp is on the B-tier of Sky Sports pundits, you will rarely see him on the Sunday 4:30pm game but he might be there for a Saturday 5:30.

He has been at Sky for a long time now having joined in 2006, he was even there in the Keys and Gray era, and is also a team captain on A League of Their Own.

Richards has fingers in many pies and so it is hard to nail down exactly what he earns.

What we do know is that he took home £205k from the BBC in their 2022 accounts but he was missing from the 2025/26 report so it must have dipped below £178k.

If we presume that it is still similar, Richards also appears on Sky and CBS, further inflating his pay packet.

To top it off, Richards is also one of the main faces on Gary Lineker’s Stick to Football podcast.

In a recent development, alan Shearer took a 50k pay cut from 2025 to 2026 but still remains one of the best-paid pundits. With the departure of Gary Lineker, he became the highest-earning sports-related pundit in the BBC but has since lost that accolade.

He’s Match of the Day’s main pundit and was co-commentator for the BBC’s coverage of the World Cup Final this summer.

Rooney became a regular Match of the Day pundit in August 2025 after numerous attempts to stay in the managerial game failed.

Signing for the BBC, he reportedly put pen to paper on a two-year £800k deal.

He was one of the key pundits for the BBC’s World Cup coverage, most memorably calling the extended half-time break “crap”, and has defied doubters to actually be a decent pundit.

He’s right now on a hiatus from his BBC deal as he is being paid a reported £800k to appear on I’m a Celeb.

Would Wayne Rooney have worked in Pep Guardiola’s Barcelona?

“It’s your job,” he famously once said, and his job pays very well.

Keane’s exact contract details are not known but he is rumoured to be earning anywhere from £500k to £1m.

That comes from both his Sky work but also his regular appearances for ITV.

The main man for Monday Night Football ranks second in the best-paid pundits.

Carragher reportedly takes home £1m a year from his Sky deal which sees him feature on every substantial game as well as plenty of others.

Unlike his partner in crime Neville, Carragher does branch out away from Sky though and is part of CBS Sports’ coverage of the Champions League for US audiences.

Neville is the face of Sky Sports’ football coverage.

He reinvented the punditry role following his retirement in 2011 and if his early Monday Night Football performances were a little too high-pitched and awkward, he soon transformed into the perfect pundit.

These days, he has jumped the shark somewhat and is becoming increasingly depressed at Manchester United but his Stick to Football podcast has been backed by Global and Disney+.

For his Sky contract alone he is reported to be taking home £1.1m a year, making him the best-paid pundit in the UK.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By RICH JONES, US DEPUTY SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 13:30 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 13:30 EST, 25 November 2026.

An English soccer star has been killed outside a Mississippi taco restaurant just months after moving to the United States to chase his dreams.

Krissh Mahatma, 18, was fatally struck by a bullet after a gun was fired outside the Green Ghost Tacos restaurant in Jackson at around 3:39 a.m. on Sunday morning.

The London-born player was with teammates from his Co-Lin Wolves team when they came across a drunk man outside the restaurant, according to Dark Horse Press.

A fight broke out and a man pulled out a gun and fired into the group, hitting Mahatma, who was taken to a nearby hospital via a private vehicle where he died, according to Hinds County Coroner Jeramiah Howard, via WLBT.

According to recent reports, capitol Police have since arrested and charged Danny Luna, 22, with murder. The Mississippi Department of Public Safety did not elaborate on what caused the deadly confrontation.

'While this arrest is an crucial step toward justice, we recognize that nothing can ease the pain of losing a loved one,' Police Chief Mark Miller said, sending 'thoughts and prayers' to Mahatma's 'family and loved ones.'.

Mahatma, who played as a striker, was in his freshman year at Copiah-Lincoln Community College in Wesson, around 45 miles south of Jackson where the incident took place.

Krissh Mahatma, 18, was fatally shot outside a taco restaurant in Jackson, Mississippi.

Danny Luna, 22, has been arrested and charged with murder after the deadly confrontation.

He had made 14 appearances in his first three months with the Co-Lin Wolves, scoring one goal in September in a 3-2 win over National Park College.

In a recent development, 'Copiah-Lincoln Community College is mourning the loss of freshman soccer player Krissh Mahatma. Krissh will be deeply missed by his teammates and the entire Co-Lin family,' Dewayne Middleton, the Co-Lin president, mentioned in a statement.

Industry observers note that before moving to the US, he had played for Watford 'A' in the post-16 Community and Education Football Alliance league. Co-Lin unveiled his signing in February.

A fundraiser set up to support his family remarked he was 'just beginning a latest chapter of life far away from home' and added: 'his sudden passing has left his family, friends, teammates, coaches, and the entire Co-Lin soccer community heartbroken.

'Behind this tragedy is a family grieving the loss of their son and loved ones trying to make sense of a loss that feels impossible to put into words.'.

Industry observers note that the owner of the Green Ghost Tacos eatery said: 'On behalf of the entire Green Ghost family, I extend my deepest and most heartfelt condolences to the family, friends, loved ones, and university community mourning the tragic loss of a young student. Our hearts are heavy, and our thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected by this devastating incident.

'While this tragedy occurred near our establishment, we would like to clarify that Green Ghost was closed and was not conducting business at the time of the shooting.

'The safety and well-being of our patrons, employees, and surrounding community remain a top priority. We are committed to cooperating fully with law enforcement as they investigate the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident.

'Out of respect for the grieving family and the investigation, we will refrain from speculating or commenting further on the details at this time.

Sources indicate that 'Above all, we recognize that a family has suffered an unimaginable loss. We ask that the community join us in extending compassion, prayers, and support to those affected during this incredibly difficult time.'.

Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, majorana zero modes provide a route to fault-tolerant qubits by encoding information non-locally in fermion parity.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, majorana zero modes provide a route to fault-tolerant qubits by encoding information non-locally in fermion parity. Their noise sensitivity is expected to decrease exponentially with separation between Majorana zero modes, a suppression known as topological protection1. Kitaev chains in quantum-dot–superconductor arrays can host Majorana zero modes at their ends1,2, even in two-site chains3. These minimal-chain modes, known as poor man’s Majoranas, retain characteristic Majorana properties, including near-zero energy and equal electron–hole character, but lack topological protection3,4,5. A key challenge is moving from identifying these modes in electrical transport to coherent qubit control. Here we demonstrate coherent time-resolved rotations between parity states encoded by four poor man’s Majoranas in two coupled minimal Kitaev chains3,6,7,8. Total fermion parity conservation separates the system into global even- and odd-parity manifolds. We observe coherent parity oscillations in both, with frequencies matching within 5% at the poor man’s Majorana sweet spot, consistent with largely isolated Majoranas6. The oscillation frequency, rotation axis and coherence depend systematically on inter-chain coupling and quantum-dot detunings, in agreement with our model for short chains. Our results establish coherent control of a qubit encoded in the fermion parity of Majorana zero modes, realized using minimal Kitaev chains. They lay the groundwork for universal qubit operations, comprehensive coherence characterization and probing protection in longer chains.

It has been revealed that a, Detailed schematic of the pulse sequence, showing the various stages of the protocol. b, p(ee∣ee), p(oo∣ee), p(ee∣oo), and p(oo∣oo) as a function of pulse duration and pulse ramp time. Parity oscillations remain visible even for slow ramp duration up to approximately 75 ns. An oscillation as a function of ramp duration is also visible at zero pulse duration, indicating that the qubit evolves partially during the ramp of the coupling pulse. c, Time trace and corresponding histogram of the readout signal \(\Delta {S}_{{\rm{M}}}^{{\rm{11}}}\) with the left chain on resonance and the right-chain QDs off-resonance, using 400 μs readout time. Transitions between \(| e\rangle \) and \(| o\rangle \) are attributed to quasiparticle poisoning. d, Dwell time histogram from c. e, p(e∣e), p(o∣e), p(e∣o), and p(o∣o) while varying the pulse amplitude VC and ramp time. For fast ramps (≲5 ns), parity mixing is observed between the chain and the dot. We attribute this to a diabatic excitation of the coupled system, which rapidly decoheres before the final measurement. In the main text, we use ramp times of 25 ns to avoid these excitations. For pulse amplitudes ≲11.5 mV, no parity mixing is observed, which we use to roughly identify when QDC passes through resonance. f, Schematic of the configuration for the measurements in c-e. g-j, Same as c-f, but for the right chain, with the QDs of the left chain off-resonance. In panel i, parity mixing between the chain and QDC is observed for ramp times  ≲ 10 ns, indicating a slightly weaker coupling between QDC and the right chain versus the left chain.

In a recent development, readout characterization using time traces of the reflected resonator signal \(\Delta {S}_{{\rm{M}}}^{{\rm{11}}}\), measured for three different amounts of detuning with the coupler QD kept fixed far from resonance. Thresholds used for single-shot state identification are obtained by fitting a Gaussian mixture model. The detuning configuration in (e-g) is used for qubit readout. a, Schematic representation of the readout configuration with both chains on resonance. b, Time trace of \(\Delta {S}_{{\rm{M}}}^{{\rm{11}}}\) and corresponding histogram for the readout configuration in a. Residual coupling between the chains results in inter-chain hopping that is faster than the readout time of 500 μs, preventing readout in a single shot. The two quantum capacitance signals corresponding to the \(| ee\rangle \) and \(| oo\rangle \) states are partially averaged which makes them difficult to distinguish from the \(| oe\rangle \) and \(| eo\rangle \) states. c, As in a, but with both chains detuned from resonance. d, Time trace of \(\Delta {S}_{{\rm{M}}}^{{\rm{11}}}\) and corresponding histogram for the readout configuration in c. The slight detuning suppresses inter-chain hopping, though it remains too fast for high-fidelity single-shot readout. Two distinctive regions can be observed: When the system is in the global even state, rapid jumps between \(| oo\rangle \) and \(| ee\rangle \) are visible. When the system is poisoned, it enters the global odd manifold. Transitions between \(| oe\rangle \) and \(| eo\rangle \) are not resolved because they produce similar readout signals. e, As in c but with both chains detuned further from resonance. f, Time trace of \(\Delta {S}_{{\rm{M}}}^{{\rm{11}}}\) and corresponding histogram for the readout configuration in e. The two computational states \(| ee\rangle \) and \(| oo\rangle \) correspond to the red and blue signals, and can now clearly be resolved. The green signal contains both leakage states of the odd global parity manifold (\(| eo\rangle \) and \(| oe\rangle \)). Due to the antisymmetric detuning where the ground state of one dot is full and the other is empty, the \(| oo\rangle \) state is energetically favored over the \(| ee\rangle \) state, resulting in a skewed population between the two. Transitions are mainly observed between the even and odd global manifolds. The signal-to-noise ratios between the leakage distribution and the \(| ee\rangle \) and \(| oo\rangle \) distributions are 2.88 ± 0.28 and 2.76 ± 0.09, respectively. Integrating the fitted Gaussian distributions across the assignment thresholds gives false-leakage probabilities of 0.45% for \(| ee\rangle \) and 0.25% for \(| oo\rangle \), showing that finite readout SNR accounts for only a small fraction of the observed leakage. g, Dwell time histogram of the three observed states, indicating the difference in lifetimes. The shortest measured state lifetime in this readout configuration is 8.3 ms, corresponding to a probability of approximately 5.8% for a state transition during the 500 μs integration window. The trace is acquired with the coupler QD kept far from resonance, showing that state switching on this timescale is already present in the readout configuration. These transitions include both residual inter-chain hopping and quasiparticle-poisoning events and can produce time-averaged signals that are assigned as leakage for pulsed measurements.

Industry observers note that conditional probabilities at the simultaneous sweet spot for the two chains in both the even and odd global parity manifolds, corresponding to Extended Data Fig. 5g but extended to larger pulse amplitudes. Additional outer lines appear when the energy of the detuned chain is aligned with the first excited state of the other chain. The quadrant in which they appear depends on the initial state of the system, as well as the global parity manifold (‘Interpretation of pulsed charge-stability diagrams’ in Methods). a, Left chain in the even manifold. b, Right chain in the even manifold. c, Left chain in the odd manifold. d, Right chain in the odd manifold. The QDR2 resonance is shifted by approximately 3 mV with respect to panel b due to the Coulomb interaction with the additional electron on the parity-switching QD. The odd-manifold measurements include two parity-switch passages, before and after the control sequence. Comparing the background return probabilities in the even- and odd-manifold measurements for initial states \(| oo\rangle \) and \(| oe\rangle \) gives single-passage parity-switch fidelity of 99.77 ± 0.03% (‘Parity-switch fidelity’ in Methods).

It has been revealed that a, Map of p(oo∣oo) (left) and p(oe∣oe) (right) as a function of the left and right hybrid-gate voltages (VLH and VRH). The diagonal and antidiagonal features of enhanced parity mixing correspond to degeneracies between the qubit basis states. The points labeled c-k indicate the VLH,VRH values used in the remaining panels. b, Schematic representation of the four configurations measured at each point: left- and right-chain pulsed charge-stability diagrams in the global even and odd parity manifolds. c-k, Pulsed charge-stability diagrams measured for the left and right chains in the even (top) and odd (bottom) parity manifolds. Unlike conventional charge-stability diagrams referenced to the Fermi energy in a normal lead, here each chain provides the energy reference for the other. As such, the measured features reflect the difference between the excitation energies of the two individual chains. Crossings are therefore observed simultaneously for the left and right chains when the splittings of the two chains compensate each other, corresponding to the qubit degeneracy condition. Consequently, the appearance of a crossing in a single parity manifold does not imply that the corresponding chain is tuned to its sweet spot. Indeed, crossing-like features are observed in only one manifold in panels c, e, i and k. The orientation of the avoided crossings depends on the parity manifold: in the even manifold, the left and right chains exhibit the same orientation, whereas in the odd manifold the orientation is reversed, reflecting the sign difference ε12 ± ε34 between the two manifolds. Only near the sweet spot (panel g) are crossings observed for both chains in both parity manifolds simultaneously, providing a unique signature that both chains are individually tuned to their sweet spots.

Industry observers note that pulsed charge-stability diagrams showing p(ee∣ee), p(oo∣ee), p(ee∣oo), and p(oo∣oo) as a function of the right-chain gate voltages (VR1, VR2), for various values of the coupler QD pulse amplitude VC for a fixed pulse duration of 10 ns. The value of VC is indicated above each panel. The device configuration is the same as in Extended Data Fig. 8. a-h, The superconducting phase difference between the chains is set to φ ≈ 0. As VC is made more negative, the coupler QD is first brought closer to resonance and parity mixing along the degeneracy lines increases. Eventually, when the coupler QD is near or below resonance (around VC = − 9 mV), the final state is dictated by the ground state of the chain in the relevant sector of the charge-stability diagram irrespective of the initial state. We note that the chain appears to move from CAR-like at low pulse amplitudes (tR < ΔR, a) across a sweet spot (tR ≈ ΔR, b-e) to ECT-like at high pulse amplitudes (tR > ΔR, f-h), which we attribute to uncompensated cross-capacitance between VC and VRH. i-n, The superconducting phase difference between the chains is set to φ ≈ π. The main difference is that the visibility of QDR2 is suppressed, as predicted by theory (Supplementary Note 4).

Unless stated otherwise, measurements are taken at VC = 9.8 mV and perpendicular field B⊥ = 15.6 mT (yellow mark in panel o), corresponding to a phase difference φ ≈ 0 between the chains. a-d, Detuning individual quantum dots. e,f, Detuning the left- (e) and right-chain QDs (f). g,h, Simultaneous detuning of the outer (g) and inner (h) QDs of both chains. i, Varying coupling pulse duration and amplitude. j, Varying VLH and VRH for a fixed pulse duration of 18 ns. The colored marks indicate sweep directions for panels k,l,p,q. k,l, Detuning the left (k) and right (l) chain via VLH and VRH. m, Oscillation frequency as a function of pulse amplitude in logarithmic scale, where V0 is the gate voltage at which QDC is on resonance. The gray line fits f = K/(V0 − VC) with K = 156.6 ± 0.3 MHz mV and V0 = 11.285 ± 0.002 mV for VC < 10.8 mV. n, Quality factor of the oscillations as a function of VC. o, Dependence on the out-of-plane magnetic field B⊥. p,q, Symmetric (p) and antisymmetric (q) detuning of VLH together with VRH.

Note that for this dataset, the chains were tuned using pulsed charge-stability diagrams but were not compared to the odd manifold. As such, it is unclear if the even and odd states of each chain are degenerate. a, Varying coupling pulse duration and amplitude VC. In contrast to the main text, QDC starts detuned below the Fermi level instead of above but is likewise pulsed closer to resonance for qubit evolution. b, Dependence on the out-of-plane magnetic field B⊥. #128995. Tech Report: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1054 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.
  • "People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW.
  • The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it.".

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Industry observers note that names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity.".

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

It has been revealed that but a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, reveals how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer mentioned their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages.".

In a recent development, research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

It has been revealed that "Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Industry observers note that even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on.".

It has been revealed that pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

Sources indicate that "People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'".

According to recent reports, later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to.".

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions.".

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'".

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point.".

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

According to recent reports, "I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there.".

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it.".

Sources indicate that that does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered.".

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny.".

Lionel Messi has scored 30 goals for Inter Miami in 2026, but he just misses out on the top 10.

Here are the 10 most prolific club goalscorers in world football this calendar year, across all competitions.

Sources indicate that A player you’ve (probably) never heard of. Get used to that.
